design_detail: Retrospective population-based cohort: Ontario residents aged 12 to 65 who answered the 2009-2010 or 2011-2012 Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS), linked at ICES to hospital, emergency department, physician-claims, mental-health and death records (data window 1 January 2009 to 31 December 2015). Exposure was any self-reported cannabis use in the 12 months before the interview; controls reported never using cannabis, or using it only once and more than 12 months earlier. Cannabis and control groups were matched up to 1 to 3 on a propensity score from 31 variables (including tobacco history and amount, problem drinking, other substance use, comorbidities and previous respiratory emergency visits) and exactly on sex, previous-year respiratory visit, tobacco smoking history and pre-existing asthma or COPD. Outcomes within 12 months of the interview: respiratory-related emergency room (ER) visit or hospital admission (primary), all-cause ER visit or admission, and all-cause death. Odds ratios by logistic regression with generalised estimating equations.
can_establish: Whether Ontario residents aged 12 to 65 who reported any cannabis use in the past year, matched to controls on 31 characteristics, differed in the odds of an emergency visit or hospital admission for a respiratory reason, for any reason, or of death, over the following 12 months.
cannot_establish: The lung effect of smoked cannabis specifically (route, amount, strength and mixing with tobacco were not asked; 42.5% of the cannabis group used less than once a month); chronic lung outcomes (symptoms, lung function, COPD) or events beyond 12 months in the main analysis; causation (observational, residual confounding possible); dose-response; results after 2015 (end of the data window) or after October 2018 (the paper says cannabis was decriminalised in Canada then); results for people under 20 or aged 50 to 65 separately (too few).

sample.recruitment: Respondents to the CCHS, a national cross-sectional survey of community-dwelling people aged 12 and over, in two cycles (2009-2010, 2011-2012); linked by coded identifiers to Ontario administrative databases held at ICES. If someone answered both cycles (about 0.2%), only the later one was used. People aged 66 and over were excluded (about 1% of the cannabis group). Survey response rate not reported in the text.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: Ontario residents aged 12 to 65. Excluded: people who had used cannabis several times but not in the past year (to keep an uncontaminated control group), and people over 65. Routes: inhalation is described as by far the most common but was not asked. Medicinal and recreational use were not distinguished.
sample.demographics: After matching, mean age 34.4 (SD 14.6) in the cannabis group and 35.2 (15.4) in controls; 42.0% women in both; 73.9% currently or formerly smoking tobacco in both (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (administrative follow-up of everyone linked). About a quarter of the cannabis group (1618 of 6425, 25.2%) found no match and was left out of the main analysis.
sample.selection_effects: Matching kept 4807 of 6425 people in the cannabis group (74.8%). Before matching, 10.3% of the cannabis group reported illicit substance use in the past year and 25.1% problem drinking, against 0.1% and 6.7% of controls; after matching both groups were at 0.7% illicit use and 17.1% to 18.3% problem drinking, so the matched cannabis group is probably one with less other drug use than the whole group (an inference; not stated by the authors). The matched controls are also unusual: 73.9% were currently or formerly smoking tobacco, against 41.3% of all controls. Survey respondents only; pre-legalisation data.

exposure.measurement: Two survey questions asked once at the interview: ever used or tried marijuana, cannabis or hashish (no; once; more than once) and, if yes, used in the past 12 months. Exposure was not updated afterwards. Route, medicinal against recreational use, quantity and potency were not collected.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency in the matched cannabis group: less than once a month 42.5%, 1 to 3 times a month 18.1%, once a week 9.4%, more than once a week 11.4%, every day 10.5%, not available 8.0%. The authors could not run a dose-response analysis because the frequency categories were too small. Route not collected.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco history and cigarettes per day, problem drinking and illicit substance use in the past year were in the propensity score; tobacco history was also matched exactly. Before matching, 79.1% of the cannabis group and 41.3% of controls were currently or formerly smoking tobacco; after matching 73.9% of each. 'Never or not available' is one tobacco category, so missing tobacco status is counted with never-smoking. Whether tobacco was mixed into cannabis was not asked.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. The authors followed outcomes for 12 months only, to limit changes in cannabis use after the interview (a 3-year analysis is in the supplement, not read).

comparison.controls: People who reported never using cannabis, or using it once and more than 12 months before the interview; people with earlier repeated use were excluded on purpose.
comparison.matching: Propensity score (31 variables: demographics, comorbidities, general health-care use, previous respiratory ER visit or admission, tobacco history and amount, problem drinking and other substance use, respirologist visits, spirometry, respiratory medicines, influenza vaccine, survey year), caliper 0.2 SD of the logit, 1 to up to 3 controls; exact matching on sex, previous-year respiratory ER visit or admission, tobacco smoking history and pre-existing asthma or COPD. All standardised differences below 0.10 after matching (largest 0.05).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not in the model: cannabis use before the past year (except for defining controls), risk-taking, injury history, secondhand smoke, occupational exposures, exercise and diet, deprivation beyond income quintile, details of other substances. Pre-exposure health care use was measured for one year.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: After matching, illicit substance use in the past year was 0.7% in both groups and problem drinking 17.1% (cannabis) against 18.3% (controls). The authors could not adjust for secondhand cannabis smoke exposure in controls.

outcomes.instruments: Administrative records: ICD-10 diagnosis codes at ER visits (NACRS) and hospital discharges (CIHI-DAD) and deaths (Registered Persons Database). Primary outcome: respiratory-related ER visit or hospital admission, with a diagnosis of upper or lower respiratory tract infection, respiratory failure, asthma or COPD (code list in the supplement, not read). Secondary: all-cause ER visit or admission, and all-cause death. All within 12 months of the interview or until death.
outcomes.validity_norms: Asthma and COPD diagnoses for matching came from validated algorithms (asthma sensitivity 84%, specificity 76%; COPD 85.0% and 78.4%). The respiratory outcome definition is the authors' own and was not validated.
outcomes.operationalization: Respiratory harm is defined as an ER visit or hospital admission coded to a respiratory diagnosis within 12 months; chronic symptoms, lung function and milder illness that does not reach the ER are not captured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three outcomes in the main analysis, then four stratified sensitivity analyses (sex, previous respiratory visit, tobacco history, asthma or COPD) of two outcomes each (mortality too few to stratify).

analysis.effect_sizes: Propensity-matched cohort (4807 against 10,395). Respiratory-related ER visit or admission: 175 events (3.6%) against 410 (3.9%), OR 0.91 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.09), p = 0.32. All-cause ER visit or admission: 1443 (30.0%) against 2699 (26.0%), OR 1.22 (1.13 to 1.31), p < 0.0001, number needed to harm 25 (the authors' calculation). All-cause death: 11 (0.2%) against 24 (0.2%), OR 0.99 (0.49 to 2.02). Respiratory outcome by subgroup: men OR 1.00 (0.77 to 1.31), women 0.86 (0.68 to 1.10); no previous respiratory visit 0.94 (0.77 to 1.14), previous visit 0.82 (0.53 to 1.26); people currently or formerly smoking tobacco 0.80 (0.65 to 0.99), p = 0.04, people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record 1.23 (0.89 to 1.70); pre-existing asthma or COPD 0.82 (0.61 to 1.11), none 0.96 (0.77 to 1.20). All-cause outcome by subgroup: men 1.23 (1.11 to 1.36), women 1.23 (1.10 to 1.37); people currently or formerly smoking tobacco 1.16 (1.06 to 1.26), people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record 1.35 (1.16 to 1.56); asthma or COPD 1.16 (1.00 to 1.35), none 1.24 (1.13 to 1.35).
analysis.covariates: Propensity score (31 variables) plus exact matching on four; no further model adjustment described.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is cited. The sensitivity analyses are described as planned. The supplement (PDF: variable definitions, ICD-10 code list, 3-year follow-up) was not opened.
analysis.selective_reporting: The conclusions rest on the secondary all-cause outcome after a null primary outcome; the 3-year analysis is reported only in the supplement. Subgroup results are given for both outcomes.
analysis.power: Not calculated. The authors say the study might be insufficiently powered for the primary outcome; the interval for the respiratory outcome runs from a 23% lower to a 9% higher odds. Deaths were too few to analyse in subgroups (11 and 24), and frequency categories too small for dose-response.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In matched adults aged 12 to 65, with a mostly infrequent-use cannabis group (42.5% less than monthly) and 12 months of follow-up, respiratory ER visits and admissions were no more frequent than in controls (3.6% against 3.9%; OR 0.91, 0.77 to 1.09), while ER visits or admissions for any reason were more frequent (30.0% against 26.0%; OR 1.22, 1.13 to 1.31). In the cannabis group's top-100-diagnosis list, trauma accounted for 15.1% of all-cause events and respiratory reasons for 14.2%; the matching list for controls is not given. Among people currently or formerly smoking tobacco the respiratory odds were lower (OR 0.80, 0.65 to 0.99), and among people who had never smoked tobacco or whose status was unknown not significantly higher (OR 1.23, 0.89 to 1.70).
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract: cannabis use 'is associated with increased risk for serious adverse health events' and "its recreational consumption is not benign". Main text: use "should be discouraged" and, in the key-messages box, the rising recreational use 'needs to be curtailed'. Gaps: (1) the designated primary respiratory outcome was null, and the policy statements rest on a secondary all-cause composite that includes any emergency visit, with trauma its largest category; (2) 'serious adverse health events' describes visits of any severity, and Table 3's footnote lists attention to dressings or sutures, repeat prescriptions and follow-up of test results among the 11.3% 'miscellaneous' reasons; (3) respiratory reasons being the second most common category among the cannabis group says nothing about excess, because the categories are not shown for controls; (4) the authors themselves say causation should not be inferred and unmeasured confounding may account for the positive finding; (5) the box describes the comparison group as people who never used cannabis, but controls included people who had tried cannabis once; (6) the recommendations (discouraged, curtailed) are not results of the study; (7) the authors write that the null respiratory result 'may certainly be real' but list factors that could hide an effect (low exposure, non-inhaled use, secondhand smoke in controls, low power), none of which the study can test, and the conclusions are drawn from the all-cause result.

timeline.event: Tashkin et al. (cited as ref 16): small study reporting more frequent protracted acute bronchitis episodes in people who smoked cannabis, as described in this paper's Introduction.

Polen et al. (cited as ref 17): more outpatient visits for respiratory illness but not more hospital admissions in people who smoked cannabis frequently and not tobacco, as described in this paper's Introduction.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of respiratory symptoms and lung function (cited as ref 4)

This study: population-based linked-data analysis of respiratory emergency and hospital use by past-year cannabis use; the authors describe the published literature on acute respiratory illness and cannabis smoking as extremely limited.

replication.where_it_stands: A single, well-linked but crude-exposure study. The authors describe the null respiratory result as somewhat at odds with the two older small studies they cite (more bronchitis episodes in one; more outpatient respiratory visits but not more hospital admissions in the other). The exposure was mostly infrequent use of unknown route. No replication is cited in the paper, and the authors say further research is needed to confirm their findings.

funding.funder: Research award grant from The Lung Association - Ontario, which received unrestricted funding from Tetra-Bio Pharma to administer the grant competition independently; ICES, funded by the Ontario Ministry of Health and Ministry of Long-Term Care; data from MOH, CIHI and Cancer Care Ontario. The paper states the funding sources had no role in the research or writing.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliations appear as numbers only in the extracted text. Tetra-Bio Pharma, the source of the grant competition's money, is described in a newswire press release about the partnership with the Lung Association (editors' lookup, not part of the paper) as a biopharmaceutical company focused on cannabinoid-based drug discovery and development; the release says the research is administered at arm's length from the funder. Funding from a cannabinoid-drug company is a reason to read the interpretation closely, not a reason to drop the findings.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort in which route, frequency, amount, product strength and tobacco co-use are recorded, with respiratory symptoms, spirometry and imaging as well as hospital use, following people who smoke cannabis without tobacco for years against people who smoke tobacco and people who use neither; plus an analysis of why the cannabis group attends emergency departments (trauma, mental health, respiratory), with the same breakdown for controls.

domains.note: Propensity matching on 31 variables including tobacco history and amount, other substances and previous respiratory visits, with exact matching on four and stratified checks; residual confounding by risk-taking, deprivation, secondhand smoke and the detail of other substances remains, and the authors say it may explain the positive finding.

One survey question on any use in the past 12 months, asked once; 42.5% used less than monthly; route, amount, strength and tobacco mixing not collected, so the exposure is only loosely related to smoking cannabis; exposure could change after the interview. The rating is for the question of smoked cannabis and lungs.

Survey respondents (response rate not given); a quarter of the cannabis group unmatched; the matched cannabis group has much less illicit drug use than the whole group, and the matched controls are unusual (73.9% with a tobacco-smoking history).
No intervention after exposure is described; the 12-month window limits drift in exposure.

The administrative databases cover all Ontario residents (single-payer plan), but the share of survey respondents who could be linked is not given in the text (Figure 1 was not extracted), item non-response in the survey is not described, and missing tobacco status is grouped with never-smoking.

Objective administrative records of ER visits, admissions and deaths, with diagnoses from ICD-10 coding; the respiratory definition was not validated, and differences between the groups in whether they seek emergency care were not examined.
No registered protocol; the headline messages come from the secondary all-cause outcome after a null primary; 3-year results are only in the supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, set by the exposure domain: the exposure is a single self-reported question about any use in the past year, which says little about smoking, amount or product, and the two groups were built by matching in a way that changed the cannabis group (less illicit drug use) and produced unusual controls. The other domains raise some concerns. The study may be cited for the odds of respiratory and all-cause emergency and hospital use over 12 months in a matched, mostly infrequent-use group, the null respiratory result with its interval, the breakdown of the cannabis group's visits and the tobacco-stratified results; not for the lung effect of smoking cannabis, for long-term or heavy use, for causation, or for the policy statements in its conclusions.

key_findings.finding: Of 35,114 Ontario residents aged 12 to 65 in the CCHS who either used cannabis in the past year or were controls, 6425 (18.3%) used cannabis in the past year; 4807 of them (74.8%) were matched to 10,395 controls (15,202 people). After matching, 73.9% of both groups currently or formerly smoked tobacco and standardised differences were below 0.10 for all variables.

Cannabis use frequency in the matched cannabis group: less than once a month 42.5%, 1 to 3 times a month 18.1%, once a week 9.4%, more than once a week 11.4%, every day 10.5%, unknown 8.0%. Route, amount and potency were not collected; the authors say inhalation is by far the most common route (citing a scoping review).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cohort derivation, 1st paragraph; Methods › Data sources; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, respiratory-related ER visit or hospital admission within 12 months: 175 events (3.6%) in the cannabis group against 410 (3.9%) in controls, OR 0.91 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.09), p = 0.32. All-cause ER visit or admission: 1443 (30.0%) against 2699 (26.0%), OR 1.22 (1.13 to 1.31), number needed to harm 25. All-cause death: 11 against 24 (0.2% each), OR 0.99 (0.49 to 2.02).
key_findings.locator: Results › Overall cohort analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Among the cannabis group's all-cause events (top 100 diagnosis codes), acute trauma was 15.1%, respiratory reasons 14.2%, gastrointestinal 13.3%, genitourinary 11.0%, muscle or joint pain 8.0%, infection 6.8%, mental health 5.4% and cardiovascular 5.4%. The same breakdown for controls is not given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overall cohort analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: The Discussion gives acute trauma as about 18%.

key_findings.finding: Respiratory outcome by tobacco history: people currently or formerly smoking tobacco OR 0.80 (0.65 to 0.99), p = 0.04 (123 events, 3.5%, against 290, 4.2%); people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record OR 1.23 (0.89 to 1.70). All-cause outcome: 1.16 (1.06 to 1.26) and 1.35 (1.16 to 1.56). By sex, respiratory OR 1.00 (0.77 to 1.31) in men and 0.86 (0.68 to 1.10) in women; by pre-existing asthma or COPD, respiratory OR 0.82 (0.61 to 1.11) with and 0.96 (0.77 to 1.20) without.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity analyses › By sex; By tobacco smoking history; By pre-existing asthma or COPD; Table 4
key_findings.note: The authors call the lower respiratory odds in people with a tobacco-smoking history surprising; it is one of several uncorrected subgroup tests.

key_findings.finding: The authors give reasons the null respiratory result may understate an effect (not adjustable): too little cannabis smoke exposure among people in the study (citing research that lung-function decline occurs only above 20 'joints per year'), some non-inhaled use, secondhand cannabis smoke in controls, and low power. They also say the large share of people in the cannabis group who used it infrequently may have contributed to the null result, that causation should not be inferred, and that unmeasured confounding might explain the positive findings.

Limitations stated: self-report (recall and social-desirability bias); no dose-response (frequency categories too small); no quantity or potency data; about 25% of the cannabis group unmatched; data only before October 2018; no secondhand-smoke adjustment; too few people under 20 and aged 50 to 65 for age-group analyses; a single province.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4, respiratory outcome by previous respiratory ER visit or admission: events in the cannabis group are 149 (no previous visit) and 33 (previous visit), which sum to 182, not the 175 of Table 2; the other splits add up (sex 81 + 94, tobacco 123 + 52, asthma or COPD 62 + 113) and so do all the control counts. In the same rows the printed percentages (3.0% and 3.5%) do not fit the counts divided by the group sizes implied by the all-cause row (our calculation: about 3.2% and 3.3%).
reporting_issues.consequence: One row of a sensitivity table is internally inconsistent and cannot be reconstructed from the text; the main result and the other subgroups are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says acute trauma was about 18% of the all-cause events in the cannabis group; Table 3 gives 15.1% (respiratory 14.2%).

The key-messages box ('What this study adds') describes the comparison group as people who never used cannabis, but the controls also included people who had used cannabis once and more than 12 months earlier (the Methods and abstract state this correctly).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor misdescription of the comparison group.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says previous research has shown lung-function decline only above 20 'joints per year' of exposure, citing Tan et al. (2019) and Pletcher et al. (2012). In CARDIA the unit is joint-years (1 joint-year = 365 joints), net FEV1 differences at 20 and 50 joint-years were not significant, and the authors say the sample was too small to confirm harm (card sc_pletcher_2012).
reporting_issues.consequence: Wrong unit and a threshold the cited cohort did not establish; do not repeat it. Tan et al. (2019) was not read here.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Never/not available' is one tobacco category in Table 1 and in the subgroup analysis.
reporting_issues.consequence: People with missing tobacco status are analysed as if they had never smoked tobacco, which weakens the 'never smokers' stratum.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC9240874 (abstract, key-messages boxes, introduction, methods, results, Tables 1 to 4 as text, figure 1 legend, discussion, funding and competing interests read; Figure 1 is an image and was not extracted; the supplementary PDF was not opened)
